title: Light and Satire
teaser: Newton publishes Opticks — light decomposed into colour. Swift publishes A Tale of a Tub — religion decomposed into absurdity. Marlborough wins Blenheim and shatters French invincibility. Locke dies in October, his empiricism unrefuted. Leibniz completes his rebuttal but withholds it. The Enlightenment sharpens its instruments.

image.alt: First edition title page of Newton's Opticks (1704)
image.caption: The first edition of Newton's Opticks (1704), published in English rather than Latin — science speaking to the educated public.

sections.art: English Baroque portraiture reaches its zenith under Godfrey Kneller, now principal painter to Queen Anne. His portraits of the monarch — unflattering, dignified, draped in ermine and royal regalia — reject Continental idealisation for a distinctly English plainness. Kneller paints what he sees: Anne's heavy features, her forceful presence. The result is propaganda through honesty. Meanwhile, Christopher Wren's St Paul's Cathedral rises toward completion (consecrated 1697, finished 1710) — the masterpiece of English Baroque architecture. Where Italian and French Baroque swirls with emotion, Wren's dome asserts mathematical clarity: the building designed by a geometer who was also an astronomer. In France, Antoine Watteau is still an unknown, working in theatrical scene-painting; his fêtes galantes lie a decade away. The Rococo is coming, but 1704 still belongs to the Grand Manner — portraits that assert status, architecture that asserts order.
sections.literature: Jonathan Swift publishes A Tale of a Tub anonymously in London — his first major work, a savage parody of religious enthusiasm and intellectual pretension. Three brothers (Peter, Martin, Jack — representing Catholicism, Anglicanism, Dissent) inherit coats they are forbidden to alter; they alter them endlessly. The allegory exposes how Christianity has been corrupted by human vanity. But Swift's real target is broader: the Moderns who believe they have surpassed the Ancients, the projectors and systematizers whose confidence outstrips their competence. The digressions overwhelm the tale — a formal joke about intellectual incoherence. Queen Anne found it blasphemous; it cost Swift any hope of episcopal preferment. He had written too well. Alongside the Tale, Swift's Battle of the Books extends the Ancient-Modern quarrel into mock-epic form. In the same year, Daniel Defoe publishes The Storm, documenting the Great Storm of November 1703 that killed 8,000 people — proto-journalism, fact gathered from witnesses. English prose is becoming instrumental: satire, reportage, argument.
sections.philosophy: On 28 October 1704, John Locke dies at Oates in Essex, aged seventy-two. The founding empiricist — who argued that the mind begins as a tabula rasa, that all knowledge derives from experience — leaves behind an intellectual revolution only half-complete. His Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) had challenged innate ideas; his political philosophy had justified the Glorious Revolution. In Hanover, Leibniz completes his New Essays on Human Understanding — a point-by-point refutation of Locke's empiricism, defending innate ideas through the metaphor of veined marble: the form pre-exists the sculptor's chisel. But when Locke dies, Leibniz withholds publication — it seems unseemly to attack a man who cannot reply. The New Essays will not appear until 1765. Meanwhile, Newton publishes Opticks — in English, not Latin — demonstrating that white light is composite, that colour is a physical property measurable by refraction. Newton waited until Robert Hooke's death in 1703 before publishing; Hooke had disputed his optical theories for decades. The dead cannot object.
sections.history: The War of the Spanish Succession turns decisively at Blenheim on 13 August 1704. The Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy crush the Franco-Bavarian army on the Danube; Marshal Tallard is captured; 30,000 French and Bavarian troops are killed, wounded, or taken prisoner. The myth of French invincibility under Louis XIV is shattered. Vienna is saved; the Grand Alliance holds. Blenheim is England's greatest continental victory since Agincourt — and Marlborough will celebrate it by building Blenheim Palace, designed by Vanbrugh, a monument to his own glory. Days earlier, on 4 August, an Anglo-Dutch fleet under Admiral Rooke captures Gibraltar — a strategic afterthought that becomes permanent: Britain still holds it. The Treaty of Utrecht (1713) will confirm both acquisitions. Queen Anne's reign, barely two years old, is defined by these triumphs; Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough, remains the Queen's closest confidante — for now.
sections.connections: The year 1704 stages a methodological revolution. Newton's Opticks demonstrates how to decompose — break white light into constituent colours, reveal the hidden structure beneath apparent unity. Swift's Tale of a Tub performs the same operation on religion and learning: beneath the seamless coat of Christian practice lie centuries of human additions, alterations, corruptions. Both works are analytical: they take apart what had seemed whole. Locke's empiricism is the philosophical foundation — knowledge built from simple ideas combined, not revealed whole from heaven. Leibniz's suppressed rebuttal argues the opposite: structure is innate, form precedes experience. The debate will shape philosophy for centuries. Blenheim, too, is a kind of decomposition: the apparently invincible French military machine broken into prisoners and corpses. The Enlightenment's method is emerging — take it apart, see how it works, rebuild from first principles. Newton with prisms, Swift with satire, Marlborough with cavalry.

funFact: Newton delayed publishing Opticks for over a decade, partly to avoid renewed disputes with Robert Hooke, who had challenged his optical theories since the 1670s. Hooke died in March 1703. Newton published in 1704. He waited.
